summary: Describes the core ideas of the Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) architecture and a protocol built on two messages, Interests and Content Objects. It specifies the mandatory and optional fields and their behavior independent of any wire encoding. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) requests data by name rather than by the address of a particular host. Forwarders route the request and keep enough information to return matching content to the requester.

questions: what is an interest in content centric networking
what is a content object in ccnx
what is the pending interest table
subtitle: A name-based request and response protocol for retrieving network content.

tldr.problem: Traditional network requests address an endpoint, while Content-Centric Networking aims to request named content from any place that can provide it.
tldr.mechanism: A consumer sends an Interest with a hierarchical name. Forwarders route by name, record the previous hop, and return a matching Content Object; an Interest Return reports certain failures.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8569 defines CCNx semantics independently of wire encoding. It is an Experimental IRTF document, not an IETF standard.

today: RFC 8569 is an Experimental IRTF document published in July 2019, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its semantics are independent of wire encoding; RFC 8609 describes a TLV encoding.

sections.title: Content Names Instead of Host Addresses
sections.content:
Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) uses hierarchical names to route requests and match responses. A consumer sends an Interest for named content; a producer returns a Content Object, and a forwarder may send an Interest Return if it cannot handle the request.

A Forwarding Information Base (FIB) tells a forwarder where to send an Interest. This RFC defines message behavior independently of wire encoding; RFC 8609 defines a TLV wire format. In CCNx 1.0, a response name must exactly match the request name.
sections.plainLanguage: A consumer asks for content by its name, not by naming a specific host. The routing system sends the request toward a place that can return matching content.

sections.title: Interests, Content Objects and Names
sections.content:
An Interest carries a name and may include a lifetime, hop limit, KeyId restriction or Content Object hash restriction. The key restriction limits the response to an object signed with a specified key; the hash restriction limits it to a matching object hash.

A Content Object carries content and may include a name, cache fields and a validation section. Names consist of typed byte-string segments, compared in binary. CCNx semantics do not require the name to be human-readable.
sections.plainLanguage: An Interest names the requested content and can restrict which response is acceptable. A Content Object carries the data and may include information used to check its integrity.

sections.title: Forwarding and Returning Content
sections.content:
A forwarder checks an Interest's hop limit, may aggregate it with similar requests, checks its optional Content Store, and then looks up the name in the FIB. It uses longest-prefix matching by name segment to choose where to forward the request.

The notional Pending Interest Table records the incoming hop, name and restrictions. When a matching Content Object arrives, the forwarder uses this state to return the response to the requester. An implementation need not use a literal table, but it must provide the specified behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: Each forwarder remembers where an Interest came from so the answer can travel back. Similar requests can share one response when their names and restrictions match.

sections.title: Validation, Caching and Matching
sections.content:
Content Objects can carry a digital signature, a message authentication code, a message integrity code, or no validation. A signature or authentication code can bind a name and payload to validation data, but the RFC leaves trust in keys to other mechanisms.

A Content Store must verify a required key or hash restriction before answering an Interest; otherwise it treats the request as a cache miss. An object should only be cached if it satisfied an Interest, which reduces the risk of cache poisoning.
sections.plainLanguage: Validation data can help a consumer check that content matches its name and has not changed. A cache must check any restriction in the request before returning stored content.

sections.title: Interest Returns and Security Limits
sections.content:
An Interest Return sends an Interest to the previous hop with a code explaining why that node cannot respond. Reasons include no route, an exceeded hop limit, congestion, prohibited access or a malformed Interest. A forwarder is not required to send or process Interest Returns.

CCNx does not specify encryption; a higher layer must provide it when needed. The RFC warns that validating signed Interests can consume resources and that caches need protection against poisoning. It also notes that binary name matching can make differing name forms significant.
sections.plainLanguage: A forwarder can return a request with a reason when it cannot process it. CCNx supports integrity checks but does not itself encrypt content or define trust in keys.
